Formula of Concord (1577)
FOR-myuh-luh uv KON-kord
noun (Lutheran confession)
From Latin formula, a set form, and concordia, agreement; named as the form that restored concord among quarreling Lutherans.

Biblical Definition

The Formula of Concord is the last of the great Lutheran symbols, drawn up in 1577 and gathered with the older confessions into the Book of Concord of 1580. It was framed to settle the bitter disputes that broke out among Lutherans after Luther's death—quarrels over free will, good works, the third use of the law, original sin, and above all the Lord's Supper. In settling these, the Formula hardened the very points at which Lutheranism stands apart from the Reformed faith. It confessed the oral eating of the true body and blood of Christ by all communicants, worthy and unworthy alike, and to defend this it embraced the doctrine of the ubiquity of Christ's human nature—that His body, by communication of the divine attributes, is present everywhere. The Reformed churches rejected both teachings. We confess that the man Christ Jesus is in heaven according to His humanity until He come again, and that the wicked, receiving the bare elements, do not receive Christ at all, while believers feed on Him spiritually by faith. The Formula also expressly condemned the Reformed understanding of the Supper as a Sacramentarian error. So while we honor the Lutherans' concern to guard against synergism and to uphold grace, the Formula marks the mature parting of the ways, and our standards lead us another road.

Webster 1828 Definition

The 1577 Lutheran symbol that resolved internal disputes, fixing the doctrines of the bodily presence and the ubiquity of Christ's humanity against the Reformed view.

FORMULA OF CONCORD, noun [Latin formula, a form, and concordia, agreement.] The last of the Lutheran confessions, drawn up in 1577 to compose the disputes within Lutheranism.

Gathered with the older symbols into the Book of Concord, 1580.

Teaches the oral eating of Christ's body by all who partake, and the ubiquity of His human nature.

Expressly condemns the Reformed doctrine of the Supper as a Sacramentarian error.

“Whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things.” Acts 3:21.

Key Scripture

Act 3:21 — "Whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things, which God hath spoken by the mouth of all his holy prophets since the world began."

Joh 16:7 — "Nevertheless I tell you the truth; It is expedient for you that I go away: for if I go not away, the Comforter will not come unto you; but if I depart, I will send him unto you."

Mar 16:19 — "So then after the Lord had spoken unto them, he was received up into heaven, and sat on the right hand of God."

Joh 6:63 — "It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life."

Modern Corruption

A Lutheran symbol whose departures from the Reformed are confessional, not a modern redefinition.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the true and abiding humanity of Christ. The Formula's doctrine of ubiquity—that Christ's body is present everywhere—dissolves the reality of His manhood, whereas Scripture says the heaven must receive Him until the restitution of all things. A body that is everywhere is no longer a body; the Reformed confession guards the genuine humanity of our ascended Lord.

The Formula also condemned the Reformed view of the Supper as Sacramentarian and taught that the unworthy orally eat Christ's very flesh. But our Lord Himself taught that the flesh profiteth nothing and the Spirit quickeneth. We confess that the wicked receive only bread to their judgment, while believers feed on the heavenly Christ by faith through the Spirit. The difference is real and we name it, even as we respect the Lutherans' stand against synergism.

Hebrew Roots

The title means the “form of agreement,” from Latin words for a set form and concord.

expand to see more

formula — Latin, a small form or fixed pattern.

concordia — Latin, agreement, harmony of hearts.

Named for the concord it sought among divided Lutherans.

Completed 1577; printed in the Book of Concord, 1580.

Its agreement was Lutheran inward, but a fence outward toward the Reformed.

Usage

"The Formula of Concord settled the Lutheran disputes by codifying the ubiquity of Christ's body."

"Because the Formula condemned the Reformed Supper, the breach between the traditions was sealed."

"Our divines answered the Formula of Concord from Acts 3, that heaven must receive Christ until He come."
